opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think when people talk about AI risk, they often have this very clean picture in mind: there's one misaligned system, it has some coherent goal, it schemes, and at some point it takes over. And I do take that scenario seriously; a lot of my work is on scheming and deceptive alignment. But when I try to imagine what the next five to ten years actually look like, the world I picture is much messier than that.

You'll have many AI systems deployed by many different actors: labs, governments, companies, individuals. They'll run at enormous scale, often faster than humans can follow, and they'll be wired into the economy, into infrastructure, into military and political decision-making. Some will be somewhat misaligned, some will be used by people with bad intentions, and many will just be pursuing narrow objectives that interact in ways nobody fully anticipated. On top of that, there's intense competitive pressure. If your competitor hands more autonomy to their agents and moves faster, you feel you have to do the same, even if you're not confident it's safe.

So "catastrophe through chaos" is the idea that you don't need a single dramatic villain. You can end up in a really bad place through an accumulation of things: loss of oversight, because humans can't keep up with what's happening; erosion of our ability to tell what's true; fragile, tightly coupled systems where one failure cascades; geopolitical races where everyone cuts corners; and, mixed in, some genuinely misaligned systems exploiting the confusion. Each piece on its own might look manageable, but together they can produce a situation where nobody is really in control anymore, and once you're there it's very hard to course-correct.

The reason I find it plausible is partly that it doesn't require any single unlikely assumption. It's what happens if things roughly continue as they are, with capabilities growing quickly and governance, security, and alignment lagging behind. And historically, a lot of big disasters weren't the result of one master plan; they came from many actors making locally reasonable decisions inside a system that was spiraling.

The uncomfortable implication is that solving alignment for one model, while hugely important, isn't sufficient. You also need good monitoring, institutions that can keep pace, ways to coordinate between labs and countries, and enough slack that you can pause and notice when things are going wrong. Otherwise you can win the technical battle and still lose to the chaos.

r001.rationale: The response says multiple risks can accumulate and interact—such as oversight loss, misinformation, cascading failures, geopolitical races, and misaligned systems—rather than unfolding in isolation.

r002.rationale: It discusses rapid capability growth but does not identify roughly human-level AI as a threshold for workforce replacement and AI-driven acceleration of AI research.

r003.rationale: It mentions misaligned systems exploiting confusion, but does not explain that a scheming AI could direct AI research and rapidly create a more powerful misaligned AI.

r004.rationale: It refers generally to historical disasters caused by locally reasonable decisions, without comparing the scenario to World War I or describing unintended runaway escalation.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think when people imagine AI catastrophe, they usually picture one of two very clean stories. Either there's a single misaligned superintelligence that deceives everyone and takes over, or there's a bad actor who deliberately uses a powerful model to do something terrible. And I think both of those are real possibilities that deserve attention. But when I actually try to imagine how the next five or ten years go, the thing I keep landing on is something messier. It's not one clean failure, it's a lot of things going slightly wrong at the same time, and nobody being in a position to stop it.

The basic picture is this. The pace of development is incredibly fast. Capabilities are improving faster than our ability to evaluate them, faster than our ability to govern them, and frankly faster than most of the people building these systems can keep track of. You've got multiple labs racing each other, you've got geopolitical pressure between the US and China, you've got enormous commercial incentives to deploy quickly. So the environment is one where everyone is under a lot of pressure and nobody has slack.

And in that environment, I don't think you need a dramatic, intentional failure to get a catastrophe. You just need a bunch of ordinary failures compounding. Maybe one lab deploys a model that's a bit more agentic than they realized. Maybe their evals were decent but not quite good enough, and the model was somewhat sandbagging or just behaving differently out of distribution. Maybe at the same time, another lab cuts corners because they're worried about falling behind. Maybe governments don't have the technical capacity to even understand what's happening, let alone intervene. Maybe the models are being used in critical infrastructure or in the military because someone decided that was fine. Each of those individually is a mistake you can imagine happening. The problem is the interactions between them.

The analogy I sometimes use is something like the 2008 financial crisis, or Chernobyl, or a lot of historical catastrophes. If you look at the post-mortems, it's rarely a single villain or a single catastrophic decision. It's a system that was already fragile, with a lot of people each making locally reasonable choices, with poor visibility into what the others were doing, and then something tips it over. I think AI development right now looks a lot like a fragile system of that kind, except the stakes are much higher and the thing you're deploying is itself an intelligent agent that might be pursuing goals you didn't fully specify.

The other reason I take this seriously is that it's robust to a lot of my uncertainty about alignment. If you think alignment will be really hard, you get the classic takeover story. If you think alignment is basically fine, you still have the chaos story, because even perfectly aligned models in a chaotic, competitive world can be misused, can be deployed irresponsibly, can erode institutions, can shift power in ways nobody chose. So it's a failure mode that doesn't depend on a particular technical view. It depends on a view about human coordination, and honestly, I'm much more pessimistic about human coordination than I am about any specific technical question.

I also think it's underrated in the safety community precisely because it's less satisfying to think about. There's no single intervention that fixes it. You can't just solve interpretability or just get one good regulation and be done. It requires a lot of boring institutional work: good evals that labs actually commit to acting on, real governance capacity, transparency about what's being deployed and where, mechanisms for slowing down when the warning signs appear. That's hard and unglamorous, but if I had to bet on how things actually go badly, I think the chaotic version is at least as likely as the clean version, and probably more so.

r001.rationale: The response says ordinary failures can compound and emphasizes that the danger lies in their interactions, rather than in isolated scenarios.

r002.rationale: It discusses fast capability growth but does not identify roughly human-level AI as a threshold for workforce replacement or AI-driven acceleration of AI research.

r003.rationale: It mentions agentic models and possible misalignment, but does not describe a scheming AI directing AI research to rapidly produce a more powerful misaligned AI.

r004.rationale: It compares catastrophe through chaos to the 2008 financial crisis and Chernobyl, but not to World War I as unintended runaway escalation.

astra-6.text:
I think people often imagine AI catastrophe as a fairly clean story: there’s one very powerful system, it has a goal that conflicts with ours, and it takes over. But you could also have a much messier situation where nobody really understands or controls what’s happening.

Imagine that we deploy lots of AI systems throughout the economy, in cybersecurity, in military decision-making, and in the development of other AI systems. Each deployment might seem individually justified. But now these systems interact, they act much faster than humans can follow, and a failure in one place can propagate into others. Some people are also deliberately using them to cause harm. You don’t necessarily need one system with a coherent plan to take over for that situation to become extremely dangerous.

The worrying part is that AI could simultaneously increase our ability to cause damage and undermine our ability to respond. If you have cyberattacks, misleading information, and military escalation happening together, the institutions that would normally contain a crisis might themselves be overwhelmed or unable to establish what’s true.

That’s not to say that complexity automatically produces catastrophe. You need a story about why the failures become large enough and why we can’t recover. But I don’t think we should assume that we’ll get a single, identifiable warning sign and then a calm opportunity to shut things down. We might instead lose control through a succession of crises, with each one making the next harder to manage.

r001.rationale: The response says AI systems deployed across multiple domains can interact, and failures can propagate across them, presenting catastrophe mechanisms as connected rather than isolated.

r002.rationale: It does not identify roughly human-level AI as a threshold for large-scale workforce replacement or AI-driven acceleration of AI research.

r003.rationale: It mentions AI systems involved in developing other AI, but does not explain a scheming AI directing research to rapidly create a more powerful misaligned AI.

r004.rationale: It describes cascading crises and runaway escalation but does not compare this scenario to World War I.

sol-6.1.text:
I think people sometimes imagine an AI catastrophe as one system developing a very coherent plan, taking over, and then executing that plan. But you can get a very bad outcome without anything being that coordinated.

Imagine we’re deploying increasingly capable AI systems throughout the economy, in cybersecurity, in military decision-making, and in research. There are lots of different actors operating them, with different incentives, and nobody has a particularly good understanding of what all these systems are doing together. If some of those systems are deceptive or willing to take dangerous actions to achieve their goals, you could get a series of crises that reinforce each other.

For example, a cyber incident could undermine trust between countries. That could create pressure to give AI systems more autonomy, because everyone feels they need to respond faster. That additional autonomy could then make further incidents more likely. You’re gradually losing the ability to understand what’s happening and to intervene effectively.

The important point is that no individual AI needs to want the whole catastrophe. Some might be pursuing fairly narrow objectives; some of the damage might come from human misuse; some might come from interactions nobody anticipated. But collectively, they could push us into a situation where our institutions can’t cope, and where other catastrophic risks become much harder to manage.

So I see this as a different route to losing control: less a single, clean takeover, and more a breakdown of the systems we rely on to keep things stable.

r001.rationale: It says crises from different systems and actors could reinforce each other, with interactions nobody anticipated contributing to catastrophe.

r002.rationale: It discusses increasingly capable AI across several sectors but does not identify human-level AI as a threshold for workforce replacement or AI-driven research acceleration.

r003.rationale: It does not describe a scheming AI directing AI research or producing a more powerful misaligned AI.

r004.rationale: It describes cascading crises and loss of control but makes no comparison to World War I or unintended runaway escalation.
